sections.h2: Who handles your Kalamazoo tax bill
sections.html:
The city splits the work. The Assessor sets values and the Treasurer sends bills. The assessor's counter is at City Hall, 241 W South Street, open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Call (269) 337-8000 or email assessor@kalamazoocity.org. Two drop boxes take payments and paperwork around the clock: one at the front of City Hall and a drive-up box on St. Johns Place at West Lovell Street.

When the local collection window closes, the Kalamazoo County Treasurer takes over any unpaid balance. Sellers get caught at that handoff, because the county adds heavier charges than the city does.

Kalamazoo is the county seat, with 73,598 people at the 2020 census and 72,683 residents in mid 2025. Renters outnumber owners here: owners live in only 42.3 percent of homes. The middle home value is $179,000 and median gross rent is $1,078 a month. Rentals, inherited houses and homes with deferred repairs often reach a sale with tax balances attached, so check your parcel on the city's BS&A Online lookup before you list. It shows tax history, payment dates, amounts due and permit history.

Each year's tax comes as two bills. Summer notices go out by July 1 and are due July 31, either in one payment or as six monthly installments that stay interest free while on time. Winter notices go out by December 1 and are due the following February 14, in one payment.

Kalamazoo city property tax calendar
DateWhat happens
By July 1Summer bills mailed
July 31Summer bill or first installment due; late payers face a one time 3% charge and 1% interest each month after
By December 1Winter bills mailed
February 14Winter bill due
March 1Anything left unpaid is delinquent and goes to the County Treasurer

The payment processor charges card users 2.8 percent with a $1.50 minimum, and electronic check users $0.85. Those fees apply online, by phone or in person.

Delinquent balances taken over by the County Treasurer carry a 4 percent administrative fee and monthly interest of 1 percent, plus costs for mailings, recording, title work and site visits. The county's sample schedule for 2025 taxes runs like this:

  • Local payment closes February 28. After that the county collects.
  • A $15 notice charge lands on October 1 of the next year.
  • The next March 1, a parcel more than a year behind is forfeited and picks up half a percent monthly interest, 6 percent retroactive interest and a $175 title search charge.
  • Recording certificates adds $60, an in person site visit $50, and the newspaper listing $50.
  • Foreclosure follows at 25 months, with ownership passing to the County Treasurer on April 1.

Once the county owns the parcel, the owner cannot take it back. A person named on the deed may claim surplus money from an auction sale, and no treasurer can waive penalties or interest.

A low income owner can ask to push the summer bill back to the winter due date. Income for the preceding year must be $40,000 or less, and the applicant must be 62 or older, the unmarried surviving spouse of such a person, blind, paraplegic, hemiplegic, quadriplegic, totally and permanently disabled, or an eligible veteran, service member, widow or widower. Applications must reach the City Treasurer's Office by September 15. There is no winter deferral.

Once a bill reaches the county, the Treasurer can set up an extension agreement at an appointment with its foreclosure prevention team. Call 269-384-8124. The county expects two tax years to be cleared each calendar year, and dangerous or condemned buildings are not eligible.

Partial payments to the county are welcome because they slow the monthly interest. Staff there also check eligibility for the principal residence, poverty and disabled veteran exemptions.

Start with the March Board of Review. MCL 211.30 sets its opening for the second Monday of March, and the city may pick the Tuesday or Wednesday after. The board sits at least 12 hours that week, including 3 hours after 6 p.m.

If the board agrees the value is off, it adjusts the assessed and taxable amounts. You get written word of the outcome by the first Monday in June, along with notice of your right to appeal further.

The next level is the Michigan Tax Tribunal, an independent tax court. Its Small Claims division hears most residential appeals in informal telephone sessions of about half an hour, and owners often appear without a lawyer. The board's notice gives the last day to file, so check it when it arrives.

A warranty deed needs two certificates. In the city, the County Treasurer will not issue one until the City Treasurer has issued one, for $10 at City Hall, 241 W South Street, phone 269-337-8036. The county certificate then costs $5 for up to 20 tax ID numbers. The state rule is MCL 211.135, which looks back five years from the deed date.

At the recording counter, 201 West Kalamazoo Avenue, the seller also owes transfer tax of $1.10 per $1,000 to the county and $7.50 per $1,000 to the state, after rounding the price up to the next $500. The deed itself costs $30 to record.

Tax owed on the house is usually paid out of closing proceeds. Ask the treasurer holding the bill for the payoff, because city and county records are updated separately.

Owners who live in their home can claim the principal residence exemption, which removes a slice of the local school operating tax. You must own and occupy the property by May 1 and file an affidavit with the Assessor.

Selling means new paperwork. The seller rescinds the exemption with the assessor, and the buyer files an affidavit of their own. Someone buying a replacement house can hold the old exemption for up to three years if the old house is vacant, listed, unleased and unused for business. The request is due May 1 following the exemption claim on the new house, and refiling by December 31 each year extends it for up to two more years.

Tell the closing agent when you moved out. A wrong exemption status on a sold house leads to corrected bills later.

If you owe back taxes, the first step is a payoff figure from whichever treasurer holds the bill: the city before March 1, the county after. Title companies pay these balances from your proceeds at closing, so a delinquent bill does not block a sale, but the extra fees listed above do come out of your pocket.

A seller who is behind and short on time can ask the county's foreclosure prevention team about an extension before listing. A cash sale to a buyer who closes quickly can also stop interest and fees from growing, since the balance is settled at the table.

faqs.q: When is the winter tax bill due in Kalamazoo?
faqs.a: February 14 of the year after billing, paid in full. Anything open on March 1 moves to the Kalamazoo County Treasurer as delinquent.

faqs.q: Can I split the summer bill into installments?
faqs.a: Yes, into six monthly payments, once the first installment arrives by July 31. A late first payment brings a single 3 percent penalty, and interest of 1 percent then accrues each month.

faqs.q: Who decides what my house is assessed at?
faqs.a: The City Assessor's Office does. If you disagree, the March Board of Review hears you first, with the Michigan Tax Tribunal as the next step.

faqs.q: Who can defer a summer bill?
faqs.a: Owners with prior year household income of $40,000 or under who are also 62 or older, blind, totally and permanently disabled, or a qualifying veteran, service member, widow or widower. The City Treasurer must receive the form by September 15.

faqs.q: How much are the tax certificates for a warranty deed?
faqs.a: Ten dollars for the city certificate and five for the county one. A parcel inside the city needs both.
